Art & Design Technology
Across the school, pupils are taught by specialist teachers in purpose-built creative spaces, including a dedicated art studio with kiln and a fully equipped DT workshop with tools and machinery. Creativity runs through daily learning and our wider Compass Curriculum, nurturing curiosity, enterprise, adventure and philanthropy in practical, exciting ways.
Art: explore, express, imagine
Your child learns to look closely, think boldly and create work they are truly proud of. Through drawing, painting, sculpture, textiles and mixed media, pupils develop fine motor skills, visual awareness and the confidence to use art as a tool for expression.
What this looks like in the classroom
Art is woven through our creative Compass Curriculum in the younger years, where themes and real-world topics inspire imaginative outcomes and deeper understanding.
Design technology: build, test, solve
In design technology, pupils become problem-solvers, inventors and engineers. They learn how things work – and how to improve them – using safe tools, modern equipment and structured guidance.
What pupils get to experience
Clubs, events and wider opportunities
Pupils can join a wide range of co-curricular activities – with around 70 clubs offered weekly across the school – including art clubs, robotics, 3D design and craft sessions that help them extend their interests further.Regular focus days, workshops and visiting specialists give children the chance to immerse themselves in bigger creative challenges and explore new mediums in a full-day format.
How art & design technology support future success
Through both subjects, pupils naturally develop the key competencies Rose Hill School values – resilience, collaboration, independence, confidence and organisation. These character habits are threaded through daily creativity and prepare your child for life.

pageCache.pageTitle: A Guide to the Transition from Prep School to Secondary School
pageCache.text:
The Transition from Prep School to Secondary School: a Guide for Parents
Moving from prep school to secondary school marks a major milestone in your child's education. This shift brings new academic demands, greater independence and a different social environment that can feel overwhelming for both children and parents.
The key to helping your child succeed during this transition lies in understanding what makes secondary school different from prep school and taking practical steps to prepare them for these changes.
The transition to secondary school can be daunting for many families, but with the right approach, you can make it smoother for everyone involved.
Here, we'll walk you through the essential steps for preparing your child, from understanding the emotional and academic challenges they may face to building their confidence and independence.
Key steps for a successful transition from prep school to secondary school
Moving from prep school to secondary school requires careful planning across several areas. Your focus should be on emotional preparation, understanding admissions requirements, selecting the right school environment and building your child's independence.
Preparing emotionally for the move
The jump from Year 6 to Year 7, or Year 8 to Year 9, brings significant changes that can feel overwhelming for children. Your child will face a new campus, different teachers and fresh social groups.
Supporting children through the transition to secondary school requires open conversations about their worries. Ask specific questions about what concerns them most, whether it's finding classrooms, making friends or managing homework.
Start building familiarity with the new routine before term begins. Practice the journey to school, visit the local area and discuss the longer school day. Many secondary private schools offer transition days where future pupils can experience their new environment.
Emotional preparation checklist:
Some children worry about increased academic pressure or getting lost on a new campus. Address these specific concerns with practical solutions and thoughtful reassurances.
Acknowledge feelings of nervousness as normal.
Share your own experiences of school transitions.
Maintain regular routines during the summer holidays.
Supporting independence, organisation and resilience
Secondary private schools demand significantly more self-management than prep schools provide. Your child will need to track multiple subjects, remember equipment and manage their own time between lessons.
Start building these skills ahead of your child starting at their new school – ideally when they are still in prep school. Create a homework station at home where your child organises their own materials. Use a planner or app to track assignments and deadlines, gradually reducing your involvement in reminders.
Independence skills to develop:
Resilience comes from experiencing small challenges and learning to overcome them. Allow your child to make minor mistakes, such as forgetting their PE kit occasionally, so they learn natural consequences in a safe environment.
Discuss problem-solving strategies for common situations: what to do if they get lost, miss the school bus, or struggle with a particular subject. Role-play these scenarios so they feel prepared.
The organisational demands increase substantially in senior school. Practice these logistics before term starts by creating similar routines at home, such as keeping track of multiple projects simultaneously.
Using an alarm clock to wake themselves.
Completing homework without constant supervision.
Asking teachers for help when needed.
Navigating new challenges and opportunities in secondary school
Secondary school brings bigger class sizes, more subjects and increased independence alongside chances to explore new interests through extracurricular activities and specialist facilities. Your child will need to adapt to higher academic demands while developing their social connections and critical thinking skills.
Academic expectations and curriculum changes
Schoolwork becomes more rigorous as students progress from Year 7 or Year 9 onwards. While prestigious secondary schools will still usually have small class sizes like prep school, expectations increase.
Your child will encounter more homework and independent study requirements. Teachers expect students to take greater responsibility for their learning and time management. The curriculum expands to include new subjects and more complex concepts that build on prep school foundations.
Key academic changes include:
longer school days with varied timetables
regular assessments and examinations
increased reading and research requirements.
Building social skills and a positive mindset
Your child will need to form new friendships while potentially maintaining old ones. The larger student body means more opportunities to connect with peers who share similar interests.
Encourage your child to join group activities during break times and lunch. Social dynamics shift as students mature. Some children thrive immediately in senior school, whilst others take longer to find their place.
Support your child by:
Talk openly about challenges they face. Help them develop resilience by viewing setbacks as learning opportunities rather than failures. The transition period varies for each child, so avoid comparing their progress to siblings or friends.
listening without immediately offering solutions
acknowledging their feelings about change
encouraging them to try new social situations
arranging meetups with classmates outside school.
Extracurricular activities and expanding interests
Secondary schools offer extensive extracurricular activities. Many independent schools provide impressive sports grounds facilities including tennis courts, swimming pools, indoor sports centres, football pitches and scenic grounds for various pursuits.
Your child can explore music, drama, debating, coding or sports teams. These activities help build confidence, teamwork and time management skills. Educational visits and residential trips provide hands-on learning experiences that complement classroom teaching.
Consider your child's interests and the extracurricular activities they took part in while at prep school when reviewing what's available. Selective secondary schools will also offer a rich extracurricular programme that allows your child to pursue the subjects they enjoy and are good at.
Importantly, quality matters more than quantity. A small number of activities your child genuinely enjoys outweigh signing up for as many activities as possible. Most independent day schools publish detailed lists of clubs and societies during induction.
Frequently asked questions
Parents often have similar concerns about academic expectations, social dynamics, emotional support, practical preparations, teacher communication and activities that help children settle into their new school environment.
How can I best prepare my child for the academic differences between prep school and secondary school?
Start by discussing how secondary school involves more subjects. Your child will need to manage homework from multiple subjects and keep track of different deadlines.
Help your child practise organising their time by using a planner or diary during the final term of prep school. Encourage them to take responsibility for packing their bag and checking they have the right books and equipment for each day.
You can also work on building independence with homework. Let your child attempt tasks on their own before offering help, as secondary school teachers expect students to try problems independently first.
Reading around subjects can build confidence before starting. If your child struggles with a particular subject, consider light revision over the summer.
What are the key social challenges my child might face during the transition to secondary school?
Your child may worry about making new friends, especially if few or no classmates from prep school are attending the same secondary school. Some children feel anxious about finding their way around a much larger campus with more students.
Friendship groups often shift during this transition. Children who were close friends at prep school might drift apart as they join different form groups or develop new interests.
Peer pressure can increase at secondary school. Your child might encounter different social expectations around appearance, behavior or activities that didn't exist at prep school.
Lunchtime and break times can feel overwhelming in a crowded environment. Some children struggle with the noise and bustle of a large dining hall or playground compared to the smaller prep school setting.
How can I support my child's emotional wellbeing throughout this change in schooling?
Listen to your child's concerns without dismissing them as trivial. Acknowledge that feeling nervous about such a big change is completely normal and many other children feel the same way.
Maintain regular routines at home, particularly around bedtime and mealtimes – consistent structure provides stability when so much else is changing in your child's life. You should also encourage your child to talk about both positive and challenging experiences from their school day. Ask specific questions about lessons, break times or lunch rather than just "How was school?"
Watch for signs of stress such as changes in sleep patterns, appetite or mood. Some children become withdrawn whilst others may show increased irritability or clinginess.
The transition can be difficult for some children according to evidence-based guidance, so don't hesitate to contact the school if you have concerns. Many selective secondary schools have pastoral staff specifically trained to support students' emotional needs.
What practical steps should I take to ensure a smooth school transition for my child?
Visit the school together before term starts if possible. Walking the route from home to school helps your child feel more confident about their journey.
Practise the morning routine during the last week of summer holidays. You could also set up a dedicated homework space at home with good lighting and minimal distractions. Your child will have more homework than at prep school and needs a proper area to work.
Arrange any necessary transport well ahead of time. Whether your child walks, cycles, takes public transport or gets a lift, they should know exactly what the plan is.
How can I communicate effectively with new teachers to support my child's adaptation to secondary school?
Attend any transition meetings or induction days offered by the school. These events provide opportunities to meet form tutors and key staff members before term begins.
Share relevant information about your child's learning style, interests or any concerns with their form tutor. Use the school's preferred communication channels, whether that's email, a parent portal or scheduled appointments.
Respond promptly to any contact from school. If a teacher reaches out about homework or behavior, take it seriously and work with them to address the issue. It's also a good idea to check the school website and any parent communications regularly for updates. Secondary schools expect parents to stay informed about events, deadlines and policies through official channels.

pageCache.text:
9 Ways a Co-Educational Prep School Prepares Children for Life
Parents today want educational settings that mirror the world their children will enter after graduation. A co-educational prep or primary school is a key way we can prepare children for the future.
Co-educational environments help children build the social skills, respect and adaptability they need to succeed in modern workplaces and communities. When boys and girls learn together from an early age, they develop natural ways of working with everyone around them.
Here, we'll explore how co-ed prep schools prepare your child for real-world success compared to single-sex schools. You'll discover the specific advantages that come from learning in a mixed-gender setting, from building communication skills to developing emotional intelligence.
1. Nurtures respect and collaboration between boys and girls
In a co-educational prep school, your child will learn to work alongside peers of all genders from an early age. This daily interaction will build essential skills they will need throughout their lives.
Boys and girls can develop mutual understanding and respect for one another when they learn together in the same classroom. Your child will naturally begin to appreciate different perspectives and recognise the value that each person brings.
Co-educational settings help children communicate and collaborate with both boys and girls regularly, an opportunity they don't get in single-sex schools. This prepares them for future workplaces and social situations where they will interact with people of all genders.
Through group projects and daily activities, pupils can practise cooperation in a natural environment. They'll learn to listen to different viewpoints and work towards common goals together.
When children learn the importance of respecting and listening to those who are different from them, they build character. These early experiences in a collaborative environment shape how your child will approach relationships and teamwork in adulthood.
2. Encourages critical thinking through diverse perspectives
When boys and girls learn together, they naturally encounter different viewpoints in classroom discussions. This creates an environment where ideas are explored from multiple angles, helping your child develop stronger analytical skills.
Your child will learn to question assumptions rather than accept information at face value. Children's critical thinking skills can strengthen when pupils examine evidence and consider alternative explanations. Co-ed classrooms provide daily opportunities for this type of intellectual growth.
Different perspectives lead to richer debates and deeper understanding. When your child hears how classmates from varied backgrounds approach the same problem, they develop more nuanced thinking patterns. This prepares them for workplaces and communities where they must collaborate with people who think differently.
Children are naturally capable of engaging with complex topics when given the right environment. A co-educational setting provides the diverse perspectives needed to sharpen these essential skills for modern life.
3. Develops strong communication and debating skills
Co-educational settings push your child to communicate effectively with peers of both genders from an early age. This daily interaction helps them learn how to express their thoughts clearly in different social situations.
When boys and girls learn together, they naturally develop confidence in expressing opinions in front of diverse audiences. Your child will practise listening to different perspectives and responding thoughtfully during co-educational classroom discussions.
Co-ed prep schools create opportunities for children to work on group projects and presentations in mixed-gender teams. These experiences will teach your child how to negotiate, compromise and articulate ideas to people with varying viewpoints.
Children can develop better socialisation and communication skills when they interact regularly with both boys and girls. Without this exposure, children may find it harder to communicate effectively in real-world settings later on.
Your child will learn to debate respectfully and present arguments confidently in co-ed settings. These communication abilities will serve them well in future workplaces and social environments where they'll need to collaborate with diverse groups of people.
4. Prepares pupils for mixed-gender workplaces
Modern workplaces bring together people of all genders working side by side. Co-educational schools prepare children for these environments by giving them daily practice interacting with peers of different genders.
When your child learns in a mixed classroom, they'll develop important workplace skills early. They'll learn to communicate effectively with everyone. This builds confidence in working with diverse teams.
UK workplaces increasingly value diversity and inclusion. Co-education aligns with workplace equality efforts by building skills that employers seek. Your child will graduate understanding how to work productively with colleagues of all genders.
This preparation gives your child a practical advantage. They enter the workforce already comfortable in mixed-gender settings, ready to contribute from day one.
5. Builds social confidence and emotional intelligence
Co-educational schools give children daily practice in interacting with peers of all genders. This regular interaction helps them develop genuine comfort in mixed social settings from an early age.
Your child can learn to express their opinions and ideas confidently in front of everyone. Research shows that co-educational environments support self-confidence, communication skills and emotional intelligence, offering a more complete education.
Children in these settings also naturally develop stronger friendship-building skills. They become comfortable making friends across gender divides, which prepares them for working with peers of different genders, backgrounds and perspectives.
Co-education also strengthens character development as well as educational development. Your child will learn to respect and listen to those who differ from them. This supports empathy and reduces conflict in their interactions.
The social skills gained in a co-ed environment translate directly to adult life. Your child will develop the emotional intelligence needed to navigate diverse workplaces and communities with confidence.
6. Promotes individuality and values differences
Co-educational prep schools create environments where your child can learn to appreciate diverse perspectives. When boys and girls study together, they encounter different approaches to problem-solving and unique viewpoints in classroom discussions.
Your child will develop their own identity while respecting others who think and act differently. This happens naturally through daily interactions with classmates of all genders.
Co-educational schools provide an early introduction to understanding and celebrating differences, whether they relate to gender, culture or personal interests. Your child will quickly learn that there isn't just one correct way to approach challenges or express ideas.
In mixed-gender classrooms, children can see firsthand that abilities and interests aren't determined by gender. Some girls excel at maths whilst some boys prefer creative writing. This exposure helps break down rigid expectations about what your child should enjoy or pursue.
The inclusive environment that comes from a co-educational system increases respect towards others and reduces discrimination. Your child will learn to judge peers based on their character and abilities rather than stereotypes. These lessons shape how they'll interact with colleagues and friends throughout their lives.
7. Teaches equality and mutual respect from early years
Co-educational prep schools introduce children to equality and mutual respect during their most formative years. Children will learn mutual respect through examples set by adults and daily interactions with diverse peers.
Your child will experience an environment where boys and girls learn together from the start. This natural mixing helps them understand that everyone deserves the same enrichment opportunities regardless of gender.
Early years settings play a key role in promoting equality amongst young children. Teachers model respectful behaviour and create situations where pupils can practise their growing social awareness.
The classroom in co-education is a space where differences are celebrated rather than ignored. Your child will learn that fairness means recognising individual needs while treating everyone with dignity.
An atmosphere where all children feel valued shapes attitudes that last a lifetime. These early lessons in equality prepare children to work collaboratively with diverse groups throughout their education and careers.
Co-educational environments naturally challenge stereotypes before they take root. Your child will develop the understanding that capability matters more than gender.
8. Enhances adaptability in dynamic social environments
Co-educational prep schools place your child in constantly shifting social situations. They learn to work with different personalities, communication styles, and perspectives daily. This frequent exposure builds flexibility, as your child will develop the ability to adjust their approach based on who they're working with and what the situation requires.
Adaptability has become a key skill as educational environments and societal demands continue to change quickly. In a co-ed setting, your child will practise this skill naturally through everyday interactions.
They'll navigate group projects with varied team members and participate in discussions where different viewpoints emerge. These experiences teach them to respond effectively when circumstances shift.
Co-education mirrors real-world dynamics, giving your child early practice in working with people of all genders. This environment helps them build resilience and adaptability that extends beyond the classroom.
9. Reflects real-world societal diversity
Co-educational schools create environments that mirror real-world communities where your child will eventually live and work. The workplace is mixed-gender, as are universities, social settings, secondary schools and most professional environments.
When your child attends a co-ed prep school, they'll experience daily interactions that prepare them for these future situations. They'll learn to communicate effectively with people of all genders from an early age. Then, when they leave in Year 6 or Year 8, they'll be prepared for secondary education and beyond.
This exposure helps your child develop essential social skills in a natural setting reflected in life outside of school. They'll see different perspectives during classroom discussions and group projects. As a result, they'll gain confidence in working alongside diverse groups of people. These experiences build a foundation for success in their future careers and personal relationships. They'll learn that everyone brings valuable ideas and skills, regardless of gender.
Frequently asked questions
Co-educational environments are the most common in both independent and state schools, and for good reason. Here, we answer some of the most commonly asked questions from parents who are considering whether co-educational education is right for their child.
What are the benefits of a coeducational environment for early childhood development?
Co-educational environments help children develop natural social skills from an early age. Boys and girls learn to communicate effectively with each other in everyday situations, which builds confidence for future interactions.
Your child will gain exposure to different perspectives and approaches to problem-solving. This diversity in thinking helps develop emotional intelligence and empathy as children learn to understand and respect different viewpoints. Children can see peers of all genders succeeding in various subjects and activities, which broadens their own sense of possibility.
How do co-educational prep schools promote social skills and equality?
Co-educational schools promote social skills and quality by allowing students to learn and socialise together in mixed classrooms, which creates opportunities for genuine friendships across genders. Your child will develop the ability to work comfortably with anyone, regardless of gender.
Daily interactions in a mixed environment teach respect and understanding. Boys and girls can learn to value each other's contributions equally in academic work, competitive sports and creative activities.
These educational institutions actively challenge gender stereotypes through their approach to all subjects and activities. Your child will see that all opportunities are open to everyone instead of fitting into gender roles, which promotes equality as a fundamental value.
What role does a co-educational prep school play in nurturing teamwork and collaboration amongst pupils?
Co-educational schools shape how your child builds friendships and approaches challenges, developing skills that carry into adult life. Working on group projects with mixed teams mirrors the reality of modern workplaces.
Your child will learn to appreciate different strengths and working styles. Boys and girls often bring varied perspectives to group tasks, which teaches flexibility and adaptability in collaborative settings.
Sports, group and team-building activities in mixed environments build social confidence. Your child can practise leadership, compromise, and mutual support in situations that reflect real-world dynamics.
